h: A great fire, a lost son and miles of trails
p: Lanhydrock's story took a dramatic turn in 1881, when a fire swept through much of the house. The family rebuilt it with the latest comforts of the time, including central heating and a new kitchen wing, which is why it feels so Victorian today. The Long Gallery, with its stunning plaster ceiling showing Old Testament scenes, survived the fire and is one of the house's highlights.

There is a poignant story here too. Tommy Agar-Robartes, the family's eldest son, was killed in the First World War in 1915, and the house tells his story in a way that brings home the human cost of the war for families across the country.
Just behind the house is the little church of St Hydroc, which gave the estate its name. It is a peaceful spot to pause after the busy rooms.

The wider estate stretches down to the River Fowey and has marked cycle trails for different abilities, from family routes to more challenging singletrack, so bring the bikes if you have them. There is plenty of space for walkers and dogs too.

Allow a full day if you want to enjoy the house, garden and estate properly. Bodmin Parkway station is close by, with a path linking the station to the estate, which makes it possible to visit without a car. Cardinham Woods is just a short drive away for more woodland adventures.
